studies.title: Secretly Sending Affection
studies.meaning: The address is to believers and the subject is a private act, not a public alliance. Affection is being sent quietly to people who had expelled the community, and the ayah names both the sending and the concealing. Its argument runs on a mismatch: those addressed had left everything for a cause, and are now leaking warmth back towards what they left. Two clauses about God knowing the hidden and the declared close the gap the secrecy assumed.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. The commentators report with broad agreement that a man of the community sent a private letter to Mecca warning of a coming expedition, and that his motive was to protect relatives still living there rather than to betray anyone. He was found out, questioned, and pardoned. The occasion is unusually well attested, and the ayah addresses the act while the surrounding passage widens it into a general principle.

keyTerms.note: From a root for love that seeks the good of its object and expresses itself in acts. It is the warmest word in this field, which is why its use here makes the passage about feeling rather than about treaties.
A verb for confiding something under the breath. The ayah uses an open verb for the same act one clause earlier and this hidden one here, so the two describe the same warmth at different volumes.
Literally the evenness of the way, a road without a rise or a dip in it. Straying from it is not described as choosing a different road but as leaving the smooth part of this one.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Almost everyone in Medina who had come from Mecca still had family there: a mother, a brother, sons who had not left. Caravans went back and forth constantly, and a letter could travel with any trader for the price of a meal. Keeping a line open to relatives was not exotic conduct; it was what any decent man in that society would have thought he owed his own blood.
studies.didYouKnow: The definite form of the word for affection used in this ayah occurs only here in the Quran. Six ayat later, the indefinite form of the same word appears as something God may yet place between the two sides. The surah warns against sending it and then holds out the possibility of its arrival, using one root for both.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage takes an inward state seriously as a matter of consequence, which is different from policing an opinion. What is described is not a belief but a direction of loyalty expressed in an act, and the act had a cost measurable in lives. Naming both concealment and disclosure in one clause removes the category of a private exception, which is exactly what the person addressed had assumed existed.

crossReferences.why: Draws the boundary of this passage seven ayat later, exempting those who never fought or expelled anyone.
Holds out the possibility of affection between the two sides, which keeps this passage from being permanent.
Warns against taking intimates from outside who never cease to wish the community harm.

studies.applyIt: Think of something you have done recently that you would not want a particular person to know about, and ask why. Sometimes the answer is ordinary privacy, which is fine. Sometimes it is that you know the two halves of your life would not survive being introduced. This ayah is only about the second kind.

studies.title: Hands And Tongues Together
studies.meaning: A short ayah supplies the evidence the previous one assumed. If they get the upper hand, three things follow: they act as enemies, they stretch out hands and tongues with harm, and they wish for the community's faith to collapse. The pairing of hands and tongues is exact, covering violence and speech as one category. The last clause moves from conduct to desire, which is what makes the description reach past any particular incident.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, supporting the instruction of the previous ayah with a statement about conduct. The community's memory of Mecca was recent and specific: years of pressure before the migration, and hostility that had continued afterwards. The commentators read this ayah as supplying the reason rather than reporting a fresh incident, and the conditional opening keeps it about what happens when circumstances allow rather than about a fixed nature.

keyTerms.note: A verb for coming upon someone and having them within reach, occurring only here in the Quran. It describes opportunity rather than intention, which is why the ayah is conditional rather than absolute.
The ordinary verb for spreading a hand open, used elsewhere of generosity. Applying it to harm is deliberate: the same gesture that gives is the one that reaches to strike.
From the same root as the word for affection this passage has just used. The surah puts warmth and hostile wishing on one root, so the contrast is between two directions of the same faculty.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A tongue could do more damage than a hand in Arabia. Satirical verse was a weapon of war, composed to be memorised and repeated at wells and markets until a man's name was ruined in every camp he might need. Tribes retained poets the way they retained warriors. Naming hands and tongues in one breath was not a figure of speech; it listed the two instruments an enemy actually used.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb for getting hold of someone in this ayah appears nowhere else in the Quran. The verb for wishing that closes it comes from the same root as the word for affection in the previous ayah, so within two ayat the identical root names both the warmth being sent and the harm being wished back.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The conditional form matters. The ayah does not say these people are incapable of anything else; it says what happens when they have the advantage, which is a claim about circumstance and character together. That leaves the door open that the surah walks through five ayat later. Ending on what they wish rather than what they do also locates the real difficulty in a place no treaty can reach.

crossReferences.why: Answers the condition described here by holding out affection between the two sides as possible.
Uses the same reasoning about people whose hatred has already shown in what their mouths let slip.
Says that whenever they overcome you they respect neither kinship nor treaty, the same conditional form.

studies.applyIt: Notice the difference between what someone has actually done to you and what you believe they would do if they could. Both may be true, but only the first is evidence. Write the two lists separately once this week for a person you find difficult. The separation usually shortens one of them considerably.

studies.title: Where The Ties Are Cut
studies.meaning: The ayah answers the motive the whole passage has been circling. The letter was written for relatives; here the relatives are named and set aside, together with children, at the one point where the account is settled. The verb chosen is not about abandonment but about separation, a cutting between people who arrive together. The closing name for God's sight returns the reader to the present, where the conduct is happening and being seen.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, in the passage responding to a letter sent to Mecca out of concern for family. The commentators emphasise that the motive was kinship rather than disbelief, which is why the answer addresses kinship directly. Arab society organised protection, inheritance and standing entirely through blood, so an argument that relatives will not help had to be made explicitly. It could not be assumed.

keyTerms.note: The plural of the word for a womb, used as the ordinary Arabic term for kin. Naming relatives by the organ that produced them keeps the tie physical, which is what makes its cancellation here striking.
A verb for making a clean division, used of separating two things that were joined and of giving a decisive verdict. Both senses are live here, since the separating and the judging are one act.

An intensive form from the root for sight, but in Arabic it covers insight as much as vision. It names someone who sees and also understands what is seen, which is why it closes an ayah about motives.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A man's womb-relations were his insurance policy. They paid compensation when he killed by accident, avenged him when he was killed, took in his widow, and fed his children in a famine year. There was no other institution doing any of that. Telling someone in that society that kin would not benefit him was not a moral observation; it was a claim about the failure of the only safety net there was.
studies.didYouKnow: The Arabic word for kinship in this ayah is the plural of the word for a womb, and it shares its root with the two names of God that open almost every surah of the Quran. The same three letters carry both the tie set aside here and the divine mercy named at the head of the Book.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage does not say kinship is worthless; it says it does not transfer. That is a precise limit, and it leaves every duty towards relatives intact while removing the idea that they can stand in for a person. What follows is a kind of moral solitude that the Quran states plainly rather than softening. And the sentence about separation is in the active voice, so the parting is done rather than merely happening.

crossReferences.why: Lists the same relations one by one at the moment each person has enough to preoccupy him.
Says no parent will avail his child and no child his parent in anything on that Day.
Places goodness to relatives among the standing obligations, which this ayah does not cancel.

studies.applyIt: Do one thing for a relative this week that has nothing to do with obligation or appearances, and do not tell anyone you did it. This ayah limits what family can do for you at the end. It does not limit what you can do for them now, and the two are easier to hold apart than people expect.

studies.title: An Excellent Example, With One Exception
studies.meaning: A model is offered and then immediately qualified. Abraham and those with him declared themselves quit of their people's worship, and the declaration is quoted in full, including a hard clause about enmity lasting until belief. Then one thing is excepted: his promise to seek forgiveness for his father. The exception is not a criticism of Abraham but a marking of what is not part of the pattern. The passage closes on his prayer of reliance.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, offering a precedent to a community torn between conviction and family in Mecca. Abraham was the ancestor the Arabs of the Hijaz claimed, which made him the one figure both sides of the conflict honoured. The commentators note that the exception about his father is explained elsewhere in the Quran, where the promise is described as made on account of a pledge and later withdrawn.

keyTerms.note: A pattern one shapes oneself by, not merely an admirable story. The phrase occurs three times in the Quran, twice in this surah of Abraham and once of the Prophet.
A noun for settled aversion rather than a flash of anger. It is paired here with the word for enmity, so the phrase covers both the feeling and the state of hostility it produces.

A verb for turning towards someone repeatedly, used of a person coming back again and again. It is gentler than the usual word for repentance and suggests a direction of travel rather than a single act.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Every tribe in the Hijaz traced itself to an ancestor and recited the line at gatherings. Abraham stood at the head of that reckoning for the Arabs of Mecca, and the sanctuary they administered was associated with him. Invoking him was not reaching for a distant figure from another people's scripture. It was naming the founder both parties claimed, and asking which of them was actually following him.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase for an excellent example occurs three times in the whole Quran. Two of the three are in this surah, at this ayah and two ayat later, both about Abraham and those with him. The third, at 33:21, uses the identical wording of the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him).
studies.theologicalSignificance: Setting an exception inside a model is unusual and consequential. It says that a figure can be exemplary without every recorded act being exemplary, which protects the reader from a flattening kind of imitation. It also preserves something tender: the promise excepted is a son's promise to a father, and the Quran does not condemn the impulse behind it. What is marked is that the promise could not be kept, not that it was wrong to feel.

crossReferences.why: Explains the excepted promise, describing it as made on account of a pledge and then set aside.
Gives the words of the promise itself, spoken as Abraham withdraws from his father's household.
Uses the identical phrase for an excellent example, there of the messenger rather than of Abraham.

studies.applyIt: Take one person you admire and name a single thing about them you would not copy. Not to diminish them, but because the exercise makes the admiration usable. This ayah does exactly that with the most honoured figure it could have chosen, and it does it in the same sentence as the praise.

studies.title: Do Not Make Us A Test
studies.meaning: The prayer asks for something indirect. Not for safety or victory, but that the community not become a trial for those who reject faith. Commentators read this two ways: that the believers not be defeated in a manner that hardens the other side, and that they not be made an instrument by which others are tested and fail. Both readings put the concern outside the person praying. Forgiveness is asked for second, and two names close it.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, completing the words attributed to Abraham and those with him and offered to the community as a pattern. The situation being addressed is one where believers were a visible minority whose fortunes were read by others as evidence about their claims. The commentators connect the prayer to that exposure rather than to a specific incident, and it is given here as words to be borrowed.

keyTerms.note: From a root for putting metal in fire to separate the pure from the dross. The word covers testing, temptation and civil strife at once, which is why the classical readings of this line diverge.
A verb for placing something into a condition or a role. The prayer does not ask to be spared a feeling; it asks not to be positioned in a particular way relative to other people.

From a root for covering something protectively, which also gives the word for a helmet. Forgiveness in this vocabulary is a covering placed over a fault rather than a declaration that nothing happened.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Reputation moved between tribes as reliable news. When a small group prospered, the story travelled that its gods or its luck were sound; when it was broken, the same route carried the opposite conclusion. Nobody in that world separated the fate of a community from the truth of what it claimed. A prayer about not becoming other people's evidence was a prayer about a mechanism everyone could see working.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for a trial in this prayer appears in ten ayat of the Quran, and its root describes the assaying of metal by fire. At 25:20 the same word is used of people being made a trial for one another, which is the exact position this prayer asks not to be placed in.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The prayer's structure says something about how faith relates to reputation. It does not ask that the community be spared hardship, and it does not ask that the other side be defeated. It asks that whatever happens should not become an argument against God in someone else's mouth. That places a believer's concern outside their own outcome, which is a demanding place to put it and an unusual one.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same word for people made a trial for one another, and asks whether they will be patient.
Records the same request in the mouths of Moses' people, using the identical phrasing.
Supplies the declaration these words conclude, spoken by Abraham and those with him.

studies.applyIt: Before your next difficult conversation, add one line to whatever you were going to ask for: that however this goes, it should not make things harder for someone watching. It is a small shift and it changes what you are willing to say. This prayer is asking for exactly that, and it asks it first.

studies.title: Perhaps Affection, Later
studies.meaning: The example is restated and its audience narrowed to whoever hopes for God and the Last Day, which makes the pattern conditional on an orientation rather than on membership. Then two names arrive for whoever turns away, one saying God needs nothing and one saying He is praised regardless. The second ayah changes the temperature entirely. Using a particle of possibility rather than promise, it holds out affection between the two sides, and closes on capability and forgiveness.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, and events in the years that followed gave the second ayah a history. Many of those the community was in conflict with at Mecca later entered the same community, and the commentators cite that development when reading this passage. The ayah itself makes no forecast. It is placed at the end of a hard instruction about loyalty, and it changes what that instruction is understood to be for.

keyTerms.note: A particle of hope and expectation, not of promise. Its presence keeps the ayah from predicting anything, which is what allows it to be read at a moment when reconciliation looks impossible.

From the root for wealth and needing nothing further. Applied to God after a mention of people turning away, it removes any suggestion that a departure costs Him something, which would make the instruction self-interested.
The indefinite form of the word the surah opened by warning against sending. It occurs three times in the Quran, once here and once of the affection God places between a husband and wife.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Feuds in Arabia ran for generations, and everyone knew examples that had outlasted the memory of what started them. They also knew how such things ended: not by argument but by a marriage, a payment, or one strong man deciding it was over. Reconciliation was a normal event in that world, arranged rather than felt, and the affection usually arrived afterwards if it arrived at all.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for affection here occurs three times in the Quran. One of the others, at 30:21, names the affection God places between spouses as a sign; the third, at 5:82, identifies those nearest in affection to the believers. The same noun therefore covers marriage, unexpected friendship, and a hoped-for end to hostility.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Placing a possibility of affection at the end of an instruction about hostility does real work. It marks the hostility as answering a situation rather than describing a permanent order, and it puts the change outside human management by making God the one who might place it. That combination asks something specific of a reader: to act on present facts without concluding anything about a person's future.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same word for the affection placed between spouses, and calls it a sign.
Opens the surah by warning against sending that same affection, which this ayah reopens as a possibility.
Names people nearest in affection to the believers, showing the category is not fixed in advance.

studies.applyIt: Think of one relationship you have written off as finished and, without contacting anyone, hold it open in your mind as a thing that might change. Not likely. Possible. This ayah uses a particle that means only that much, and it puts it at the end of the harshest passage in the surah.

studies.title: Kindness Is Not Withdrawn
studies.meaning: The ayah is framed as a negative, which changes its force. It does not command kindness; it removes any supposition that kindness had been ruled out. Two conditions define who it covers: those who did not fight over religion and did not take part in an expulsion. For everyone in that description, two things are named, dutiful kindness and equity, and the second is the one God is said to love. The love clause makes the equity the point.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, arriving seven ayat after a warning about loyalty and drawing its boundary. The commentators report that the ayah answered real uncertainty: believers had relatives and old associates in Mecca and elsewhere who had taken no part in the fighting, and people were unsure how to treat them. Reports name different individuals as the occasion, and the Quran states the category rather than the case.

keyTerms.note: From the root behind the word for dutiful goodness, the same one used of how a person treats parents. Choosing it here sets the standard at family conduct rather than at mere civility.

A verb for giving each side its due share, from a root that also yields the word for a portion. It occurs only here in this form, and it names fairness in dealings rather than a feeling towards someone.

The Quran names only a small number of groups as loved by God, and this is one of them. The phrase occurs three times, each closing a passage about dealing fairly with people on the other side of a conflict.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Conflict in Arabia was rarely total. A tribe at war with another still traded with its allies, still married across the line where old ties held, and still honoured guests from the wrong side. Neutral parties were common and their neutrality was respected because everyone needed it eventually. The distinction this ayah draws, between people who fought and people who did not, was a familiar one in practice.
studies.didYouKnow: The closing phrase, that God loves those who act equitably, occurs three times in the Quran, at 5:42, 49:9 and here. In the other two it follows an instruction about judging between disputing parties. Here it follows an instruction about people on the other side of a war, which is the widest of the three settings.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Two criteria are named and both are about conduct: fighting and expelling. Belief is not one of them. That means the boundary in this passage runs along what people did rather than what they hold, which is a narrower line than a reader arriving at the surah might expect. And by attaching God's love to equity specifically, the ayah makes fairness towards an opponent a matter of relationship with God rather than of policy.

crossReferences.why: States the other half of the boundary in the next ayah, naming exactly who is excluded and why.
Instructs that hatred of a people not prevent anyone from acting justly, the same principle put positively.
Ends with the same declaration about God loving the equitable, after an instruction on reconciling.

studies.applyIt: Take a group you have opinions about and pick one person in it you actually know. Ask yourself whether you have ever treated them worse than you would treat a stranger, on account of the group. If so, correct one small thing this week. This ayah draws its line around conduct, not around categories.

studies.title: The Line Drawn Precisely
studies.meaning: The restriction is stated with a particle meaning only this and nothing more, and then three conditions are listed: they fought over religion, they expelled you, and they backed the expulsion. The third clause is the careful one, because it reaches people who never lifted a weapon but lent their weight. Even then, what is named is taking such people as patrons, not every kind of dealing with them. The verdict falls on whoever does it.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, paired with the ayah before it so that the two together define a boundary from both sides. The Meccan opposition had included people who never fought but funded, sheltered or agitated, and the community knew exactly who they were. The commentators treat the two ayat as one provision, and note that the restrictive particle at the head of this one is what keeps the previous ayah's permission in force.

keyTerms.note: A restrictive particle that fences a statement to exactly what follows. Its position at the head of the ayah is what prevents the restriction from spreading beyond the three conditions listed after it.
Built on the word for a back, so it means putting one's back behind an effort. It occurs only here in the Quran, and its root also supplies the estranging formula addressed two surahs earlier.

From the root for closeness and for the relation between a patron and a client. The verb names an alliance with obligations attached, which is narrower than friendship and much narrower than courtesy.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Patronage in Arabia was a formal status, not a warm feeling. A client attached himself to a patron and gained protection; the patron gained a follower and answered for him. Everyone knew who was whose, and the arrangement was announced publicly. What this ayah names is that arrangement, which is why it does not touch ordinary trade, hospitality or family contact happening at the same time.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb for lending support in this ayah occurs nowhere else in the Quran. It is built on the word for a back, and the same root produced the estranging formula addressed two surahs earlier, at 58:2. One root therefore supplies both a man turning his back on a marriage and a group putting its back behind an expulsion.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage refuses to work by group. It lists acts, and it lists three of them rather than one, which means someone can fall outside the restriction by not having done any of them. That precision does real moral work, because a rule stated by category would have been easier to apply and would have caught people who had done nothing. The cost of the precision is that it has to be read carefully.

crossReferences.why: States the other half of the boundary, covering everyone who did not fight or take part in an expulsion.
Notes believing men and women in Mecca whom the community did not know, which is why a blanket rule would have failed.
Distinguishes those who withdraw and offer peace, resting the difference on conduct rather than on a name.

studies.applyIt: When you next find yourself explaining why you cannot deal with someone, count the specific things they have actually done. If the list is short and the feeling is large, that gap is worth sitting with. This ayah takes the trouble to name three separate acts rather than settling for a name.

studies.title: Not Sent Back
studies.meaning: A situation is addressed in which women arrived in Medina alone, having left households in Mecca. The passage directs that their claim be examined and, if it holds, that they not be returned. What follows is a settlement of accounts in both directions: what husbands had paid is repaid to them, and the same claim runs the other way. The commentators read the examination as verbal rather than intrusive, and the ayah closes by calling the whole arrangement God's ruling.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, after the treaty of Hudaybiyyah, which included a clause returning to Mecca anyone who came over to Medina. The commentators agree that women began arriving under that arrangement and that this passage addressed their case. It is among the better attested occasions in the surah. Reports differ on individuals and on how the examination was conducted, and the Quran describes neither.

keyTerms.note: From a root for testing metal or sifting grain, occurring only here in the Quran. The surah takes its name from this word, in the passive form: the woman who is examined.

The feminine plural of the participle for one who cuts ties and departs, occurring only here in the Quran. Applying it to women in their own right makes the departure their act rather than a household's.

The plural of a word for something one grips for safety, from the root for protection. Using it of a marriage tie pictures the relationship as a handhold, which is why the verb beside it is holding on.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A woman who left Mecca alone travelled a route of several days without an escort and arrived where she had no kin to answer for her. In that society she had no standing of her own anywhere. Marriage payments were real property, often a herd or its value, and a household that lost both a wife and the payment had suffered a loss the community recognised. Both facts had to be handled at once.
studies.didYouKnow: Four words in this single ayah occur nowhere else in the Quran, including the verb for examining, from which the surah takes its name, and the feminine plural for women who have emigrated. The phrase calling something God's ruling appears twice in the Book, here and at 5:43.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage settles a conflict between a treaty and a person, and it settles it in the person's favour while compensating the other side. That combination is the interesting part: nothing is confiscated and nobody is simply overruled. A woman's own account of what she believes is treated as the decisive evidence, examined but not overridden, and the clause noting that God knows her faith better than anyone limits how far the examination can reach.

crossReferences.why: Mentions believing men and women in Mecca unknown to the community, the situation these arrivals came out of.
Addresses the treatment of women within marriage, insisting on kindness and on not coercing them over property.
Handles another case where a marriage ends and a payment has to be settled graciously.

studies.applyIt: Think of a rule you follow that would produce an unjust result for one particular person you know. Notice that you can usually see it clearly when it is a face rather than a category. This passage does the same work: it holds an agreement and a person together and looks for the arrangement that damages neither.

studies.title: Making The Other Side Whole
studies.meaning: The reverse case is addressed. Where the movement went the other way and a marriage payment was lost with it, the passage directs that the man be compensated from what came in. Nothing is said about pursuing anyone or about blame. It is an accounting instruction, and it closes on mindfulness of God, which is the note that keeps a financial remedy from becoming an occasion for grievance. Commentators differ over the exact mechanism.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, completing the provision of the previous ayah by handling the case running in the opposite direction. Under the treaty, movement happened both ways and the other side did not always return what had been paid. The commentators describe a practical impasse rather than a grievance about loyalty, and read this ayah as a remedy internal to the community, drawn from what was already in its hands.

keyTerms.note: A verb for something getting past someone and being gone, used of a missed opportunity as much as a lost object. It carries no accusation, which is consistent with an ayah that assigns no blame.

From the root for what follows behind, and it occurs only here in the Quran. Commentators differ over whether it means taking a turn, exacting a penalty, or a later gain arriving, and translations preserve the range.

A word for exact correspondence rather than approximate fairness. It sets the compensation at the same amount rather than at a punitive one, which is what keeps the provision a repair rather than a reprisal.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A marriage payment was often the largest single transfer a young man made in his life, sometimes years of savings or a substantial part of a family's herd. Losing it was not a symbolic injury. In ordinary circumstances a man in that position would have gone to his wife's kin and pressed the claim, and if they refused, the matter escalated through the tribe. Here neither route was open.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb at the centre of this ayah occurs only once in the whole Quran, and its meaning was contested from the earliest period. Classical readings include taking one's turn, exacting a penalty, and receiving something afterwards, and the major translations still divide along the same three lines today.
studies.theologicalSignificance: A grievance is answered by a transfer rather than by a licence to retaliate, which is the shape of the whole passage. The man who lost something is made whole from a common pool, so the cost of an unreachable wrong is spread across the community instead of pursued against a person. Closing on mindfulness of God addresses the temptation the remedy creates, since a claim to be repaid is easy to inflate.

crossReferences.why: Handles the case running the other way, with the same insistence that both sides be repaid what they spent.
Sets a response at the measure of the injury, the same principle of an equivalent rather than an excess.
Keeps a repayment equal to the harm and then prefers pardon, which is the register this ayah shares.

studies.applyIt: If you are owed something by someone you will never realistically recover it from, try naming the exact amount once, out loud or on paper, and then deciding what you will do with the fact. Vagueness keeps a grievance alive longer than a number does. This ayah answers a loss by fixing its size first.

studies.title: The Pledge And Its Terms
studies.meaning: A pledge is described with its content set out in full: no associating anything with God, no theft, no unlawful sex, no killing of children, no fabrication about parentage, and no disobedience in what is right. The list is notable for what it contains and for its last clause, which limits the obligation to what is good. The instruction that follows is twofold: accept the pledge, and ask forgiveness for those making it.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. The commentators connect this ayah with the pledges taken from women at various points, including at the conquest of Mecca, and they report that the pledge was verbal rather than by hand. Reports differ on the occasions and the individuals. What is agreed is that women gave their allegiance directly and in their own names, which the ayah records without comment as ordinary.

keyTerms.note: From the root for a sale, since a pledge of allegiance was struck like a bargain with a clasp of hands. This feminine form occurs only here in the Quran, and the transaction language is the ordinary one.

From a root meaning to leave someone dumbfounded. The word names a lie so brazen it stops the hearer, and it occurs in this indefinite form only here, describing a claim made about a child's parentage.
Literally the known, meaning what a decent society already recognises as good. Placing it at the end of the pledge attaches a limit to the obedience promised, since the pledge covers only that.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: The killing of infant daughters is attested in pre-Islamic Arabia and is condemned elsewhere in the Quran in plain terms. A household under famine pressure, or facing the cost of a daughter's future marriage negotiations, sometimes made that choice. Naming it inside a pledge, alongside theft, addressed something the people taking the pledge would have known about in families near their own.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb for women giving a pledge occurs only here in the Quran. Its list of terms overlaps with the one at 6:151, which is addressed to everyone: both begin with associating nothing with God, and both name the killing of one's children and the avoidance of indecency among the things renounced.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The pledge is taken from women directly, without a male relative standing between them and the commitment, and the Quran presents this as unremarkable. That matters more than any argument about it would. The closing limit on obedience is equally consequential: allegiance is promised only in what is recognised as good, so the pledge builds its own boundary into itself. And the response commanded is not congratulation but a request for forgiveness.

crossReferences.why: Sets out an overlapping list addressed to everyone, opening with the same term about associating nothing with God.
Asks the buried infant girl for what offence she was killed, addressing the practice named in this pledge.
Describes a pledge given to the messenger as a pledge given to God, in the same commercial vocabulary.

studies.applyIt: Notice that the pledge ends by limiting itself, and that the person receiving it is told to ask forgiveness for those who give it. If you lead anything, borrow both halves this week: name what your authority does not cover, and think well of the people under it. Neither takes long, and together they change the room.

studies.title: Despairing Of Both Ends
studies.meaning: The surah closes by returning to its opening subject and adding a reason. The people warned against are described by a state rather than an act: they have given up on the Hereafter. Then a comparison arrives whose sense the commentators divide over. It may mean they despair as the faithless despair of the dead ever returning, or as those already in the graves despair of any good. Both readings make despair the description rather than hostility.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, closing the surah with the same address it opened with and the same instruction. Between the two stand the example of Abraham, the boundary drawn around conduct, and the provisions about women who had arrived. The commentators do not attach a fresh occasion to this ayah; they read it as the seal on the whole surah, restating the instruction and supplying a diagnosis that had not yet been given.

keyTerms.note: A verb for giving up on something as no longer possible. The Quran elsewhere treats despair of God's mercy as the serious failing, and this ayah applies the same verb to despair of the Hereafter itself.

A phrase occurring only here in the Quran. The word for occupants usually names companions or people belonging to something, so the buried are described as belonging to their graves rather than merely lying in them.
The plain verb for anger, stated of God in the past tense so that it names a settled condition rather than a flaring. The same four-word phrase appeared two surahs earlier, at 58:14.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Graves in Arabia were shallow and close by. A settlement buried its dead at the edge of the palms, and people walked past them daily going out to work. Burial was quick and the ground was left plain. The dead were near enough to be part of the landscape and absent enough that nobody expected anything of them. That ordinary assumption is what the comparison in this ayah reaches for.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase naming the occupants of the graves occurs only here in the Quran. The surah's final ayah opens with the same address to believers as its first, and describes the people in question with a four-word phrase used earlier at 58:14, so the closing line ties the surah to itself and to an earlier one at once.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Despair is treated as the underlying condition rather than as a consequence, which reorders the whole surah. Hostility, broken promises and shifting loyalty have all been described, and here the root of them is named as having stopped expecting anything beyond this life. That is a generous diagnosis in one sense, since it treats the conduct as following from a belief. It is also the bleakest description in the surah.

crossReferences.why: Describes the same group with the identical phrase, in a passage about oaths sworn to a falsehood.
Answers despair directly, telling those who have wronged themselves not to give up on God's mercy.
Opens the surah with the same address and the same instruction, which this ayah closes by repeating.

studies.applyIt: Notice where you have quietly stopped expecting anything to change, and how your behaviour has adjusted around that. Despair rarely announces itself; it shows up as no longer bothering. Pick one thing you have stopped bothering about and do the smallest version of it today. That is the reverse of what this ayah describes.
